aldemar.headline: The consumer cracks and the chip trade wobbles — but the banks quietly work
aldemar.standfirst: Friday broke the streak: retail sales fell 0.6% and Michigan sentiment came in at 51 against 54.5 expected, and the S&P slipped 0.17% from Thursday's record to 7,785.76. The damage was concentrated where the AI money is — Applied Materials led a semiconductor selloff despite beating, Broadcom fell 6% after BofA questioned a $370 billion debt financing arrangement, and INTC gave back 2.0% of Thursday's spike. Your three new entries landed into that: both BAC positions are green, both INTC positions are red, and the interim deal on Hormuz expires Tuesday.

positions.title: 1 signal on BAC — read before the open (INTC quiet)

items.html: BAC — The long end sells off to a 25-year high — the 30-year auction clears at 5.216%. That is the steepener a bank balance sheet is built for: funding costs anchored at the front, asset yields repricing at the back, and net interest margin widening in between. BAC closed 64.49, up 0.62% on a day the S&P fell — the relative strength that a pullback entry wants to see. Gabriel is +0.17% on entry at 0.03R; Aldemar +0.51% at 0.07R. The counterweight is Friday's consumer data: retail sales −0.6% and sentiment at 51 are a credit-quality question for a bank with a large card book, and it is the risk this thesis carries.

BAC — "Bull signal flashing for bank stock" — a chart-pattern note on BAC. Technical commentary that arrives after the move rather than before it. You already have your levels: support around 62, resistance at 65 — and Friday's high of 64.55 stopped just under that resistance, which is the level that matters now.

INTC — INTC −2.0% to 102.50 as Applied Materials leads a chip selloff. Sector profit-taking, not a change in the case: AMAT fell despite beating, and Intel was sold on valuation caution after Thursday's run rather than on any Intel-specific news. Thursday's high of 107.57 and Friday's 102.07 low bracket the giveback. Gabriel is −2.89% on entry at −0.30R with the stop 6.8% below at 95.52; Aldemar is −3.13% at −0.13R, his 81.10 stop sitting 20.9% below — a wide stop that keeps the dollar risk near Gabriel's on a single share, and buys the full-cycle hold his thesis asks for. Worth noting rather than acting on: its own put wall sits at 105, and Friday closed underneath it.

positions.note: Signal changes the thesis, the levels or the size — earnings, a regulator with teeth, M&A, a ruling with a revenue line attached. Everything else is filed as noise on purpose; a real signal survives skepticism.

themes.right: blockade indefinite · interim deal expires Tuesday
themes.title: Trump floats annexing the strait as a fresh carrier group sails — three days to the deadline

items.html: Trump says he will declare the Strait of Hormuz US territory "pretty soon". A maximalist position taken three days before the interim deal lapses, and the opposite of the language a negotiation normally uses at this stage. It raises the odds that Tuesday passes without an extension.

A replacement carrier group sails for the region to relieve the USS Lincoln. Rotation, not reinforcement — but it is the physical proof behind Hegseth's "indefinitely". The blockade now has a scheduled relief, which is what permanence looks like operationally.

The Treasury chief signals economic measures against Iran "never seen" before. Escalation on the financial track while the naval one holds. For oil this is supply-negative at the margin; for the deadline it is one more reason Tehran walks rather than signs.

WTI closed 81.84, up 0.73% on the day and 4.7% on the week. Energy was Friday's best sector while tech was its worst — the war premium is quietly rebuilding even as equity indices drift. Crude, not the headlines, is the honest gauge of what the market expects Tuesday.

themes.note: The transmission is oil → inflation → the regime call, and this week every link loosened except the last. CPI and PPI both cooled, and Friday's retail sales and sentiment misses pushed September to a hold — but crude added 4.7% on the week, which is exactly what keeps CPI y/y at 3.3 above the 2.5 floor and Policy tightening alive. Tuesday resolves the argument: an extension takes the premium out, a lapse puts it back on with the blockade live. You are long a bank into a steepening curve and long a chipmaker into a risk-off tape, so both sides of that outcome touch the book.

world.title: A record on Thursday, a reality check on Friday — and a third straight weekly gain anyway

items.html: Retail sales −0.6% m/m; Michigan sentiment 51 against 54.5 expected. The first genuinely weak consumer prints of the run, and they cement a September hold. Disinflation arriving through a softening consumer is a different story from disinflation arriving through cheaper energy — it is better for bonds than for earnings.

Broadcom −6% after BofA questions a $370bn debt financing arrangement; AMAT leads chips lower despite a beat. The third instalment of the same story that took Alphabet down on Tuesday: the market has started auditing how AI infrastructure is paid for. Beating estimates is no longer enough if the balance sheet carries the build.

The 30-year auction clears at 5.216%, the highest in 25 years; the 10-year eases to 4.69%. A steepening curve driven by the long end — deficits and energy, not policy. It is a headwind for long-duration equity and a tailwind for lenders, which is precisely the rotation Friday's tape showed.

S&P −0.17% to 7,785.76, Nasdaq −0.28%, but the Russell 2000 rose 0.51%. Small caps and energy up while megacap tech fell is a breadth rotation, not a risk-off day. The VIX at 14.25 agrees — this was repositioning, not fear.

weekly.headline: The week the market started auditing the AI bill — and the war stopped pretending
weekly.standfirst: Five sessions, a third straight weekly gain, and a record close on Thursday: the S&P added 0.36% to 7,785.76 while the VIX fell to 14.25. Underneath that calm, two things changed. Investors began pricing how AI infrastructure is financed rather than what it might earn — Alphabet on Tuesday, Broadcom and Applied Materials on Friday — while the CPU side of the same trade got re-rated upward. And the war moved from rhetoric to enforcement: a US helicopter disabled a tanker running the blockade, Hormuz traffic sank to three-month lows, and the interim deal now expires on Tuesday.
